questions.question: What is Jetpack Compose, and how does it differ from the traditional Android View system?
questions.title: What is Jetpack Compose, and how does it differ from the traditional Android View system?

sections.heading: Jetpack Compose
sections.content: Jetpack Compose is Android's modern declarative UI toolkit. Differences from traditional Views:

items: Declarative vs Imperative: Compose describes what UI should look like.
Less boilerplate: No XML layouts.
Reactive: UI updates automatically when state changes.
Composables: UI elements are Kotlin functions.
Works seamlessly with existing Android components.

sections.heading: Jetpack Compose

questions.question: Explain the concept of declarative UI in Jetpack Compose.
questions.title: Explain the concept of declarative UI in Jetpack Compose.

sections.heading: Declarative UI
sections.content: In declarative UI, you describe the UI for a given state instead of specifying steps to update it.

sections.heading: Note
items: Compose automatically updates UI on state changes.

sections.heading: Example

questions.question: Declarative UI vs Imperative UI
questions.title: Declarative UI vs Imperative UI

sections.heading: Imperative UI:
items: Describes how to update UI step-by-step
Used in XML + View system
Requires manual UI updates

sections.heading: Declarative UI:
items: Describes what UI should display based on state
Used in Jetpack Compose
UI updates automatically

sections.heading: In Short:
items: Imperative = Manual updates
Declarative = State-driven UI

questions.question: What are Composable functions?
questions.title: What are Composable functions?

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: Composable functions are the basic building blocks of UI in Jetpack Compose. They are functions marked with the @Composable annotation that define how the UI should look.

sections.heading: Key Features
items: Used to create UI components
Can be combined (composed) to build complex layouts
Automatically update UI when state changes
Written using Kotlin functions instead of XML

sections.heading: Example

questions.question: What are the benefits of Jetpack Compose?
questions.title: What are the benefits of Jetpack Compose?

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: Jetpack Compose is Android's modern UI toolkit that lets developers build UI using Kotlin instead of XML, making development faster and simpler.

sections.heading: Benefits
items: Less Code – Removes XML layouts and reduces boilerplate.
Faster Development – Declarative UI with live previews speeds up development.
Easy Theming – Built-in Material Design and dark mode support.
Reusable UI – Composable functions improve modularity and maintainability.
Better State Management – UI updates automatically when data changes.
Improved Performance – Smart recomposition updates only necessary UI parts.
Interoperability – Works with existing XML Views for gradual migration.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.content: Compose simplifies Android UI development with cleaner code, better performance, and faster UI creation.

questions.question: Jetpack Compose vs Android View System
questions.title: Jetpack Compose vs Android View System

sections.heading: Comparison
items: Feature: UI Approach | Compose: Declarative | View System: Imperative
Feature: Layout | Compose: Composables | View System: XML + Views
Feature: State Handling | Compose: Automatic recomposition | View System: Manual updates
Feature: Boilerplate | Compose: Less | View System: More
Feature: Interoperability | Compose: Works with Views | View System: Views can host Compose via AndroidView

questions.question: Explain the role of @Composable in Jetpack Compose.
questions.title: Explain the role of @Composable in Jetpack Compose.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: @Composable turns a Kotlin function into a UI function that builds and updates UI in Jetpack Compose.

sections.heading: Defines UI Components
sections.content: Used to create UI elements like text, buttons, layouts, or screens.

sections.heading: Enables Declarative UI
sections.content: Describes what UI should look like. UI updates automatically when data changes.

sections.heading: Supports Recomposition
sections.content: Only affected composables are redrawn when state changes, improving performance.

sections.heading: Allows UI Composition
sections.content: Composable functions can call other composables to build reusable and complex UI.

questions.question: Explain the lifecycle of a Composable.
questions.title: Explain the lifecycle of a Composable.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: The lifecycle of a composable defines how it is created, updated, and removed from the UI in Jetpack Compose.

sections.heading: Composition
sections.content: When a composable is first called, Compose creates the UI and adds it to the screen.

sections.heading: Recomposition
sections.content: When the state used inside a composable changes, Compose re-executes the function and updates only the required UI parts.

sections.heading: Disposal
sections.content: When a composable is no longer needed, it is removed from the UI and its resources are cleared.

sections.heading: State Awareness
sections.content: Compose tracks state changes automatically, ensuring the UI stays updated and efficient.

questions.question: How do you handle lifecycle events in Compose functions?
questions.title: How do you handle lifecycle events in Compose functions?

sections.heading: Lifecycle Handling
items: LaunchedEffect → Run suspend code when key changes
DisposableEffect → Cleanup resources
SideEffect → Run after successful composition
Observe LifecycleOwner using LocalLifecycleOwner.current

sections.heading: Example

questions.question: What is State in Compose?
questions.title: What is State in Compose?

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: State in Jetpack Compose represents data that can change and affect the UI. When state changes, Compose automatically updates the UI.

sections.heading: Holds UI Data
sections.content: Stores values like text input, selection, or visibility.

sections.heading: Triggers UI Updates
sections.content: State changes automatically recompose and update the UI.

sections.heading: Managed with State APIs
sections.content: Handled using tools like remember and mutableStateOf.

sections.heading: Enables Reactive UI
sections.content: Helps create dynamic UI that responds to user actions and data changes.

questions.question: How does state management work in Jetpack Compose, and what are the common state types?
questions.title: How does state management work in Jetpack Compose, and what are the common state types?

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: State management in Jetpack Compose controls how UI data is stored, updated, and observed. When state changes, Compose automatically recomposes and updates the UI.

sections.heading: How State Management Works
sections.content: Compose observes state values used inside composable functions. When the state changes, only the affected UI is recomposed.

sections.heading: remember
sections.content: Stores state inside a composable and survives recomposition.

sections.heading: mutableStateOf
sections.content: Creates observable state that triggers UI updates when changed.

sections.heading: rememberSaveable
sections.content: Saves state across configuration changes like screen rotation.

sections.heading: State / MutableState
sections.content: Wrapper classes that hold and observe state values.

questions.question: What is MutableState and how does recomposition happen?
questions.title: What is MutableState and how does recomposition happen?

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: MutableState is a state holder in Jetpack Compose that stores a value and notifies Compose when the value changes.

sections.heading: What is MutableState?
sections.content: A wrapper around a value that can be observed and updated, usually created using mutableStateOf.

sections.heading: How Recomposition Happens
sections.content: When the state value changes, Compose re-executes composables using that state and updates only the affected UI.

sections.heading: Benefit
sections.content: Helps create reactive UI with automatic and efficient updates.

questions.question: Stateful composable vs Stateless composable
questions.title: Stateful composable vs Stateless composable

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: In Jetpack Compose, composables can be stateful or stateless depending on whether they hold or rely on state.

sections.heading: Stateful Composable
items: Holds its own state using remember or mutableStateOf.
Responsible for updating itself when the state changes.
Example: A text field that manages its input internally.

sections.heading: Stateless Composable
items: Does not hold state internally.
Receives state and events via parameters.
Relies on parent composables to manage state.
Example: A button that displays a value passed from its parent.

questions.question: Difference between Stateless and Stateful composables
questions.title: Difference between Stateless and Stateful composables

sections.heading: Stateful Composable
items: Holds and manages its own state.
Updates itself when the state changes.
Less reusable due to internal state.
Example: A TextField managing its input internally.

sections.heading: Stateless Composable
items: Does not hold state; receives state from parent.
UI updates rely on external state changes.
Highly reusable and easier to test.
Example: A Button displaying text passed from parent.

questions.question: What is State Hoisting?
questions.title: What is State Hoisting?

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: State Hoisting in Jetpack Compose is moving state up to a parent composable, making the child stateless and reusable.

sections.heading: How It Works
items: Parent holds the state and passes it to the child.
Child emits events to update the parent's state.

sections.heading: Benefits
items: Makes UI components reusable and testable.
Separates state management from UI.
Enables unidirectional data flow.

sections.heading: Example

questions.question: How to retain state across recomposition and configuration changes?
questions.title: How to retain state across recomposition and configuration changes?

sections.heading: Across Recomposition
items: Use remember to keep state during recomposition.

sections.heading: Across Recomposition
sections.code: var count by remember { mutableStateOf(0) }

sections.heading: Across Configuration Changes
items: Use rememberSaveable to retain state during recomposition and rotations.

sections.heading: Across Configuration Changes
sections.code: var count by rememberSaveable { mutableStateOf(0) }

sections.heading: Key Difference
sections.content: remember → recomposition only. rememberSaveable → recomposition + config changes.

questions.question: What is Recomposition?
questions.title: What is Recomposition?

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: Recomposition in Jetpack Compose is the process where a composable function is re-executed to update the UI when the state it depends on changes.

sections.heading: How It Works
items: Compose tracks state used in composables.
When the state changes, only the affected composables are recomposed.
Unaffected parts of the UI are not redrawn, improving performance.

sections.heading: Benefits
items: Ensures UI is always in sync with data.
Provides efficient and reactive updates without manual UI refresh.

questions.question: How to avoid recomposition of a composable if the state is not changed? (Smart Recomposition)
questions.title: How to avoid recomposition of a composable if the state is not changed? (Smart Recomposition)

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: To prevent recomposition when state hasn't changed:

sections.heading: remember
items: remember – Keeps state across recompositions.

sections.code: val value = remember { computeValue() }

sections.heading: key
items: key – Recompose only when the key changes.

sections.code: key(user.id) { UserProfile(user) }

sections.heading: derivedStateOf
items: derivedStateOf – Recompose only if the derived value changes.

sections.code: val derivedValue by remember { derivedStateOf { state1 + state2 } }

sections.heading: Note
items: Immutable/Stable Data – Helps Compose skip recomposition if the value is unchanged.

questions.question: Does re-composition of ComposeItem1 affect ComposeItem2? If yes, how?
questions.title: Does re-composition of ComposeItem1 affect ComposeItem2? If yes, how?

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: No, recomposition in Jetpack Compose is localized.

sections.heading: How It Works
items: Compose tracks which state each composable uses.
If ComposeItem1's state changes, only ComposeItem1 is recomposed.
ComposeItem2 remains unaffected if it doesn't depend on the same state.

sections.heading: Key Point
items: Only composables that observe changed state are recomposed.
This makes Compose efficient by avoiding unnecessary UI redraws.

questions.question: What are stable types that can skip recomposition?
questions.title: What are stable types that can skip recomposition?

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: Stable types are objects or values that don't change unexpectedly, allowing Compose to skip recomposition when they remain the same.

sections.heading: Stable Types
items: Primitive types: Int, Float, Boolean, String
Immutable collections: List, Map, Set from Kotlin's immutable types
Objects marked with @Stable
Functions / Lambdas that don't capture changing state

sections.heading: Key Point
items: If a composable uses only stable types, Compose can avoid recomposing it when unrelated state changes, improving performance.

questions.question: What are side effects in Compose?
questions.title: What are side effects in Compose?

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: Side effects in Compose are operations that interact with the outside world or cause changes outside the composable scope, such as updating state, launching coroutines, or performing I/O.

sections.heading: Examples of Side Effects
items: Showing a Toast or Snackbar
Navigating to another screen
Writing to a database or shared preferences
Launching coroutines for API calls

sections.heading: Handling Side Effects
items: LaunchedEffect – Runs a coroutine tied to the composable lifecycle
SideEffect – Runs after every successful recomposition
DisposableEffect – Cleans up resources when the composable leaves composition

questions.question: Difference between LaunchedEffect and DisposableEffect
questions.title: Difference between LaunchedEffect and DisposableEffect

sections.heading: LaunchedEffect
items: Runs a coroutine tied to composable lifecycle.
Used for async tasks (API calls, animations).
Cancels automatically when key changes or composable leaves.

sections.code: LaunchedEffect(userId) { fetchUserData(userId) }

sections.heading: DisposableEffect
items: Runs side effects with cleanup when entering/leaving composition.
Used for resources or listeners.

questions.question: What is rememberCoroutineScope and its use cases?
questions.title: What is rememberCoroutineScope and its use cases?

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: rememberCoroutineScope is a Compose API that provides a lifecycle-aware CoroutineScope tied to a composable. It allows launching coroutines from UI events like clicks or gestures.

sections.heading: How It Works
items: Returns a CoroutineScope that cancels automatically when the composable leaves the composition.
Unlike LaunchedEffect, it can be used inside event handlers (e.g., button clicks).

sections.heading: Use Case

questions.question: How to launch a coroutine from a composable function (LaunchedEffect)?
questions.title: How to launch a coroutine from a composable function (LaunchedEffect)?

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: LaunchedEffect lets you launch a coroutine tied to a composable's lifecycle. It cancels automatically when the key changes or the composable leaves.

sections.heading: Note
sections.content: Use Case: Initial data loading, animations, or side effects in composables.

questions.question: How to launch a coroutine from a non-composable function but tied to composition (rememberCoroutineScope)?
questions.title: How to launch a coroutine from a non-composable function but tied to composition (rememberCoroutineScope)?

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: rememberCoroutineScope provides a lifecycle-aware CoroutineScope that can be used in event handlers or non-composable functions inside a composable.

sections.heading: How It Works
items: The scope is tied to the composable's lifecycle.
Cancels automatically when the composable leaves composition.
Useful for launching coroutines imperatively (e.g., on button click).

sections.heading: Example

questions.question: How to observe Flows and LiveData states in Compose UI?
questions.title: How to observe Flows and LiveData states in Compose UI?

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: Compose provides extension functions to convert Flows and LiveData into Compose State, so the UI automatically updates when new values are emitted.

sections.heading: Observing Flow
items: Use collectAsState() to collect a Flow as Compose State.
Requires a coroutine scope internally — safe to use in composables.

sections.heading: Flow Example
sections.code:
val uiState by viewModel.uiStateFlow.collectAsState()
Text(text = uiState.message)

sections.heading: Observing LiveData
items: Use observeAsState() from the lifecycle-compose library.
Automatically starts and stops observation based on composable lifecycle.

sections.heading: LiveData Example
sections.code:
val uiState by viewModel.uiStateLiveData.observeAsState()
Text(text = uiState?.message ?: "Loading")

sections.heading: Key Points
items: collectAsState() → for StateFlow / Flow
observeAsState() → for LiveData (add lifecycle-compose dependency)
Both return a State<T> that triggers recomposition on change.

questions.question: How can we handle asynchronous operations in Jetpack Compose?
questions.title: How can we handle asynchronous operations in Jetpack Compose?

sections.heading: LaunchedEffect
items: Best for triggering async work when a composable enters composition or a key changes.
Automatically cancelled when key changes or composable leaves.

sections.heading: LaunchedEffect Example
rememberCoroutineScope
items: Best for launching coroutines from user interactions (button clicks, etc.).
Scope is tied to composable lifecycle.

sections.heading: rememberCoroutineScope Example
ViewModel + collectAsState
items: Best practice: handle async logic in ViewModel, expose results as StateFlow, collect in Compose.

sections.heading: ViewModel + Flow Example
sections.code:
val uiState by viewModel.uiState.collectAsState()
Text(text = uiState.message)

questions.question: How can we convert a non-compose state into a Compose state?
questions.title: How can we convert a non-compose state into a Compose state?

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: Non-Compose state sources like Flow, LiveData, or RxJava observables can be converted into Compose State using adapter functions so they trigger recomposition automatically.

sections.heading: Flow → Compose State
items: Use collectAsState()

sections.heading: Flow Example
sections.code: val state by myFlow.collectAsState(initial = "")

sections.heading: LiveData → Compose State
items: Use observeAsState()

sections.heading: LiveData Example
sections.code: val state by myLiveData.observeAsState(initial = "")

sections.heading: RxJava / Custom Observable → Compose State
items: Use produceState() to produce State from any async or callback source.

sections.heading: produceState Example
Key Takeaway
items: collectAsState() → Flow / StateFlow
observeAsState() → LiveData
produceState() → Any async source or callback

questions.question: Explain derivedStateOf.
questions.title: Explain derivedStateOf.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: derivedStateOf is a Compose API that creates a derived state from one or more state objects. The derived state is only recomputed when the underlying state it depends on actually changes, preventing unnecessary recompositions.

sections.heading: When to Use
items: When a value is computed from other state values.
When you want to avoid recomposing a composable unless the derived value itself changes.
Common for filtering, mapping, or computing lists based on other state.

sections.heading: Example
Key Point
items: Without derivedStateOf, the list would recompute on every recomposition.
With it, recomposition is skipped if the derived value hasn't changed.

questions.question: Explain rememberUpdatedState.
questions.title: Explain rememberUpdatedState.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: rememberUpdatedState is used to capture the latest value of a parameter inside a long-running effect (like LaunchedEffect) without restarting the effect when the value changes.

sections.heading: Why It's Needed
items: LaunchedEffect restarts only when its key changes.
If a lambda or value inside it changes, the effect won't restart — it captures the old value.
rememberUpdatedState ensures the latest value is always available inside the effect without restarting it.

sections.heading: Problem without rememberUpdatedState
With rememberUpdatedState
Key Use Cases
items: Timers or delays where the callback may change.
Long-running effects that reference frequently changing lambdas.

questions.question: Difference between remember and rememberSaveable.
questions.title: Difference between remember and rememberSaveable.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: Both remember and rememberSaveable are used to persist state across recompositions, but they differ in what events they survive.

sections.heading: remember
items: Stores state in memory during composition.
State is lost when the composable leaves the composition.
State is also lost on configuration changes (rotation, dark mode toggle).
Use for temporary state that doesn't need to outlive the screen.

sections.heading: remember Example
sections.code:
var count by remember { mutableStateOf(0) }
// count is lost on screen rotation

sections.heading: rememberSaveable
items: Stores state that survives recomposition AND configuration changes.
Uses Bundle under the hood (like saved instance state).
Works with primitive types and Parcelable/Serializable objects.
Use for state that should be retained across rotations or process death.

sections.heading: rememberSaveable Example
sections.code:
var count by rememberSaveable { mutableStateOf(0) }
// count survives screen rotation

questions.question: What are the best practices for performance optimization in Jetpack Compose?
questions.title: What are the best practices for performance optimization in Jetpack Compose?

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: Compose is efficient by default, but following best practices ensures minimal unnecessary recompositions and smooth UI performance.

sections.heading: Key Practices
items: Use stable types — Compose can skip recomposition for composables with stable/immutable parameters.
Use derivedStateOf — Compute derived values only when the source state actually changes.
Avoid reading state in the wrong phase — Read state as late as possible (in draw phase, not measure).
Use keys in LazyList — Provide stable keys to LazyColumn/LazyRow to avoid full list recomposition.
Hoist state up — Keep composables stateless where possible for better reuse and skipping.
Use @Stable and @Immutable annotations — Mark data classes to help Compose know they won't change unexpectedly.
Avoid creating lambdas inside composables — Lambda creation on each recomposition causes unnecessary allocations. Use remember or define outside.
Use lazy loading — Use LazyColumn/LazyRow instead of Column/Row for long lists.

sections.heading: Stable key in LazyColumn

questions.question: Can we use both Jetpack Compose and Android View in a Single App?
questions.title: Can we use both Jetpack Compose and Android View in a Single App?

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: Yes. Jetpack Compose and the traditional View system can coexist in the same app. This is called interoperability, and it allows gradual migration from Views to Compose.

sections.heading: Embedding Compose inside a View
items: Use ComposeView inside an XML layout to host composables.

sections.heading: ComposeView in XML
Embedding a View inside Compose
items: Use AndroidView composable to embed traditional Views inside a composable.

sections.heading: AndroidView in Compose
Key Points
items: ComposeView → embed Compose inside XML/View hierarchy.
AndroidView → embed traditional Views inside Compose.
Ideal for gradual migration — no need to rewrite entire apps at once.

questions.question: Explain CompositionLocal
questions.title: Explain CompositionLocal

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: CompositionLocal is a Compose mechanism that allows you to pass data implicitly down the composable tree without manually passing it as parameters to every composable.

sections.heading: Why It Exists
items: Passing the same data (like theme, locale, or user context) through every composable is verbose.
CompositionLocal provides a scoped, implicit data channel down the tree.

sections.heading: Defining a CompositionLocal
sections.code: val LocalUser = compositionLocalOf<User> { error("No user provided") }

sections.heading: Providing a value
Consuming the value
Built-in Examples
items: LocalContext.current — Access Android Context
LocalDensity.current — Access screen density
MaterialTheme.colorScheme — Uses CompositionLocal internally

questions.question: Explain Jetpack Compose Phases.
questions.title: Explain Jetpack Compose Phases.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: Jetpack Compose renders UI in three distinct phases: Composition, Layout, and Drawing. Understanding these helps write more efficient composables.

sections.heading: Phase 1 — Composition
items: Compose executes composable functions to build the UI tree.
State is read here — any state read during composition triggers recomposition when changed.
Output: a tree of composable nodes.

sections.heading: Phase 2 — Layout
items: Each composable node is measured and positioned.
Two steps: measure children, then place them on screen.
Modifiers like size(), padding(), fillMaxWidth() are applied here.

sections.heading: Phase 3 — Drawing
items: Each composable node is painted on the screen.
Background colors, text, images, borders are drawn here.
Canvas-based drawing (drawBehind, drawWithContent) happens in this phase.

sections.heading: Performance Tip
items: Reading state in the Drawing phase (via graphicsLayer or drawBehind) avoids triggering Composition and Layout, improving performance.
Example: Animating alpha with graphicsLayer skips recomposition entirely.

sections.heading: Example — Reading state in Drawing phase
sections.code:
val alpha by animateFloatAsState(if (visible) 1f else 0f)
Box(Modifier.graphicsLayer { this.alpha = alpha }) { // Drawing phase only
    Text("Hello")
}

questions.question: What is the role of the Modifier in Jetpack Compose?
questions.title: What is the role of the Modifier in Jetpack Compose?

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: Modifier is a core concept in Jetpack Compose used to decorate or add behavior to composables — such as size, padding, background, click handling, and more — without modifying the composable itself.

sections.heading: What Modifier Does
items: Adjusts size, padding, margin, and alignment.
Adds background colors, borders, and shapes.
Handles gestures (clickable, draggable, scrollable).
Controls visibility, clipping, and elevation.
Chains multiple behaviors together in order.

sections.heading: Example
Key Points
items: Modifier order matters — padding before background differs from background before padding.
Pass Modifier as a parameter to make composables reusable and flexible.
Always start with the incoming modifier: Modifier = Modifier.

questions.question: What are Semantics?
questions.title: What are Semantics?

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: Semantics in Jetpack Compose define the meaning of UI elements for accessibility services (like TalkBack) and UI testing. They attach metadata to composables so assistive tools know what each UI element represents.

sections.heading: Two Main Uses
items: Accessibility — Screen readers use semantics to describe UI elements to users with disabilities.
Testing — UI tests use semantics to find and interact with composables.

sections.heading: Adding semantics via Modifier
Using semantics in UI tests
sections.code:
composeTestRule
    .onNodeWithContentDescription("Company Logo")
    .assertIsDisplayed()

sections.heading: Key Points
items: contentDescription is the most common semantic property.
Use mergeDescendants = true to group related elements for accessibility.
clearAndSetSemantics {} overrides all child semantics.

questions.question: How can you handle user input and events in Jetpack Compose?
questions.title: How can you handle user input and events in Jetpack Compose?

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: Jetpack Compose handles user input and events through Modifiers and composable event callbacks, following a unidirectional data flow pattern.

sections.heading: Click Events
items: Use Modifier.clickable {} or Button's onClick parameter.

sections.heading: Click Example
Text Input
items: Use TextField with onValueChange to handle text input.

sections.heading: TextField Example

questions.question: How do you handle navigation in Jetpack Compose?
questions.title: How do you handle navigation in Jetpack Compose?

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: Jetpack Compose uses the Navigation Compose library (androidx.navigation:navigation-compose) to handle in-app navigation between composable screens.

sections.heading: Setup
items: Add dependency: implementation("androidx.navigation:navigation-compose:x.x.x")
Create a NavController using rememberNavController().
Define a NavHost with routes and composable destinations.

sections.heading: Basic Navigation Example

questions.question: How do you handle orientation changes in Jetpack Compose?
questions.title: How do you handle orientation changes in Jetpack Compose?

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: In Jetpack Compose, orientation changes (configuration changes) cause the composable to be re-created. State must be properly persisted to survive these changes.

sections.heading: Persisting State with rememberSaveable
items: Use rememberSaveable instead of remember to retain state across rotations.
Works automatically for primitive types and Parcelable/Serializable objects.

sections.heading: rememberSaveable Example
sections.code:
var count by rememberSaveable { mutableStateOf(0) }
// count survives screen rotation

sections.heading: Using ViewModel
items: The recommended approach is to keep state in a ViewModel.
ViewModel survives configuration changes automatically.
Expose state as StateFlow and collect in Compose.

// ViewModel state survives rotation

questions.question: Explain the concept of unidirectional data flow in Jetpack Compose.
questions.title: Explain the concept of unidirectional data flow in Jetpack Compose.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: Unidirectional Data Flow (UDF) is a pattern in Jetpack Compose where state flows down the composable tree, and events flow up. This makes UI predictable and easy to debug.

sections.heading: How It Works
items: State flows DOWN — parent passes state to child composables.
Events flow UP — child composables notify parent via callbacks.
The parent decides how to update state in response to events.

sections.heading: Example
Benefits
items: Single source of truth — state is owned by one place.
Easier to test and debug — UI is a pure function of state.
Enables State Hoisting — children become stateless and reusable.

questions.question: How to create Custom Layouts in Compose?
questions.title: How to create Custom Layouts in Compose?

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: Jetpack Compose allows creating fully custom layouts using the Layout composable. This lets you control how children are measured and positioned when built-in layouts (Column, Row, Box) are not sufficient.

sections.heading: Basic Custom Layout Example
